name: Bronx Zoo
short_description: World-famous, largest US zoo by acreage/animals; tier-5-scale tourist anchor. Quick gravity: very high.

_pipeline.address: Fordham Rd. and Bronx River Pkwy., Bronx
_pipeline.discovery_notes: World-famous, largest US zoo by acreage/animals; tier-5-scale tourist anchor. Quick gravity: very high.

beats.script_body: If you count number of animals as well as acreage, the Bronx Zoo is the largest zoo in the United States. With over 4,000 animals and 24 exhibits, it requires strategy to see what you want without meltdowns from the younger set. Expect to spend an entire day here — you'll need it.

beats.script_body: Make a direct path first to the Congo Gorilla Forest, a remarkable exhibit of silverback gorillas that begins with a short film. Once the film is over, curtains dramatically part to reveal floor-to-ceiling windows, with cavorting gorillas galore. Unlike other animals at the zoo, the gorillas are always awake if you visit in the daytime, and along with the adults there always seem to be half-a-dozen baby gorillas in sight as well.

name: Brooklyn Museum
short_description: Major encyclopedic art museum; world-class Egyptian collection. Quick gravity: high.

_pipeline.address: 200 Eastern Pkwy. (at Washington Ave.), Brooklyn
_pipeline.discovery_notes: Major encyclopedic art museum; world-class Egyptian collection. Quick gravity: high.

beats.script_body: The Brooklyn Museum's Egyptian Collection, while not as extensive as the Met's, arguably has more masterpieces. When an ancient Egyptian piece comes up at auction, dealers often ask, 'Is it Brooklyn quality?' — the museum's collection being the benchmark for this sort of artifact. Among its wonders are a tiny 5,000-year-old, pre-dynastic terra cotta sculpture of a woman, nicknamed 'Birdwoman' for her beaklike face, and the Cartonnage of Nespanetjerenpere, a mummy case whose colors are electrically bright and unfaded.

beats.source_passage: Its Egyptian Collection, while not as extensive as the Met's, arguably has more masterpieces. (When an ancient Egyptian piece comes up at auction, dealers often ask, “Is it Brooklyn quality?”—the Brooklyn Museum's collection being the benchmark for this sort of artifact.) Among the collection's many wonders are a tiny 5,000-year-old, pre-dynastic terra cotta sculpture of a woman, which curators have nicknamed “Birdwoman” for her beaklike face, one of very few intact sculptures from this long-ago era. The Cartonnage of Nespanetjerenpere is another highlight, a mummy case that looks like it was swiped from the set of Revenge of the Mummy, its colors electrically bright and unfaded.

name: Brooklyn Navy Yard
short_description: Historic 300-acre industrial complex with free museum. Quick gravity: medium-high.

_pipeline.address: East River waterfront (btw. Williamsburg and Manhattan bridges); Museum at Building 77, 141 Flushing Ave., Brooklyn
_pipeline.discovery_notes: Historic 300-acre industrial complex with free museum. Quick gravity: medium-high.

beats.script_body: At its peak during World War II, when it employed some 70,000 men and women, the Brooklyn Navy Yard was the biggest industrial complex in U.S. history — no other site has yet topped that employment figure. The oral histories of the women who worked here during the war, preserved at the on-site museum, are especially moving.
key_claims: At WWII peak employed ~70,000 and was biggest industrial complex in US history
On-site museum preserves oral histories of women workers
beats.source_passage: At its peak usage during World War II, when it employed some 70,000 men and women, the Brooklyn Navy Yard was the biggest industrial complex in U.S. history—no other site has yet to top that employment figure.

fact_check.notes: Superlative 'biggest industrial complex in U.S. history' — left to fact-check; never auto-resolve.

beats.script_body: The Yard's importance to America began far earlier, during the American Revolution, when the British docked their infamous prison ships here. Conditions aboard them were so atrocious that more than 11,500 Americans perished — more than the combined U.S. casualties in all the battles of the Revolution. Most of their bodies were simply dumped overboard into the water, making these waters the largest Revolutionary graveyard in the States.

name: Green-Wood Cemetery
short_description: Historic 1837 arboretum-cemetery; notable interments. Quick gravity: medium-high.

_pipeline.address: Main entrance Fifth Ave. at 25th St., Sunset Park, Brooklyn
_pipeline.discovery_notes: Historic 1837 arboretum-cemetery; notable interments. Quick gravity: medium-high.

beats.script_body: As you wander New York, you'll notice streets named for important Gothamites you'll also encounter at Green-Wood. The city's 'first families' were all interred here, along with such notables as DeWitt Clinton — a presidential candidate and mastermind behind the Erie Canal — composer Leonard Bernstein of Broadway's West Side Story, and artists Louis Comfort Tiffany and Jean Michel Basquiat.
key_claims: First families and notables interred: DeWitt Clinton, Leonard Bernstein, Louis Comfort Tiffany, Jean Michel Basquiat
beats.source_passage: The “first families” of the city were all interred here, as were such notables as DeWitt Clinton (a presidential candidate who was the mastermind behind the Erie Canal), Leonard Bernstein (composer of Broadway's West Side Story), and artists Louis Comfort Tiffany and Jean Michel Basquiat.

beats.script_body: Even pets were buried here — until the funeral of a devoted horse convinced the cemetery's staff to stop the practice in 1870. The cemetery itself was founded in 1837.

beats.source_passage: Heck, even pets were buried here . . . until the funeral of a devoted horse convinced the cemetery's staff to stop the practice in 1870 (the cemetery itself was founded in 1837).

beats.script_body: It's not hard to understand why New Yorkers would pick Green-Wood for their eternal rest. Set on the highest point of Brooklyn, it's a stunning place, considered an arboretum as well as a cemetery for the 7,000 or so trees that grow here. The monuments are equally beautiful, hand-carved in dozens of styles, from Tiffany-glass-adorned mausoleums to bronze and marble statuary.

name: Industry City

_pipeline.address: Btw. 33rd St. and 41st St., from Gowanus Expressway to waterfront, Brooklyn (Sunset Park)
_pipeline.discovery_notes: Rehabbed warehouse entertainment/shopping complex. Quick gravity: medium.

beats.script_body: The 16-building complex was first developed by Irving T. Bush in the 1890s as a multi-use manufacturing and warehouse site. By the 1970s much of it had become derelict, but then, as happened in the SoHo and Dumbo areas, it was rehabbed by artists. Alas, just as in those two neighborhoods, private developers priced out the artists, and most have had to move to cheaper spaces.

name: New York Aquarium
short_description: Coney Island aquarium; post-Sandy Ocean Wonders shark center. Quick gravity: medium-high.

_pipeline.address: 502 Surf Ave. (at W. 8th St.), Coney Island, Brooklyn
_pipeline.discovery_notes: Coney Island aquarium; post-Sandy Ocean Wonders shark center. Quick gravity: medium-high.

beats.script_body: In 2012, the surge from Hurricane Sandy effectively swamped the New York Aquarium. Its sea lions and most of the other aquatic critters surfed the storm unhurt, but the buildings were heavily damaged, new construction was put on hold, and visitors could only see 40% of the facilities. That changed in the summer of 2018, when the whiz-bang Ocean Wonders center opened.

beats.source_passage: In 2012, the surge from Hurricane Sandy effectively swamped the New York Aquarium. Its sea lions and most of the other aquatic critters were able to surf the storm unhurt, but the buildings were heavily damaged, new construction was put on hold, and visitors were only able to see 40% of the facilities. That changed in the summer of 2018, when the whiz-bang Ocean Wonders center opened.

beats.script_body: The Ocean Wonders center is dedicated to sharks and the Grand-Canyon-deep underwater 'Hudson Canyon,' which lies just 40 miles off the city's coastline. It doubled what there is to see at the aquarium, with great whites, leopard sharks, giant rays, and endangered Atlantic sturgeons in massive walk-through tanks, plus interactive exhibits on sustainable seafood, ocean trash, and the importance of sharks to the ecosystem.

name: Isamu Noguchi Garden Museum

_pipeline.discovery_notes: Only US museum founded by an artist in his lifetime; Zen sculpture garden. Quick gravity: medium.

beats.script_body: Utterly unique, this is the only museum in the nation founded by an artist in his lifetime, dedicated to his work and curated by him. Because Noguchi, who lived from 1904 to 1988, was a genius across sculpture, architecture, ceramics, and furniture design, he was more than up to the task, creating a space at once balanced and often rapturously beautiful.

beats.script_body: The no. 7 train — which originates at Times Square and snakes mostly above ground through the heart of ethnic Queens — is popularly known as the International Express. Built by immigrants in the early 1900s, the no. 7 IRT brought those same immigrants to homes on the outer fringes of the city, and that tradition has continued as newcomers settle close by its elevated tracks. Get off in Sunnyside for Romanian groceries, in Jackson Heights for Indian saris and Sikh turbans, or ride to Flushing, where Queens's Chinatown is bigger than Manhattan's. In 1999 it was nominated as a National Millennium Trail and chosen to represent the American immigrant experience.
key_claims: The no. 7 train is known as the International Express
Built by immigrants early 1900s; passes ethnic Queens neighborhoods (Sunnyside, Jackson Heights, Flushing)
Nominated 1999 as a National Millennium Trail, chosen to represent American immigrant experience
beats.source_passage: The no. 7 train—which originates in Manhattan at Times Square, makes three stops in that borough, and then snakes, mostly above ground, through the heart of ethnic Queens—is also popularly known as the International Express. Built by immigrants in the early 1900s, the no. 7 IRT (Interborough Rapid Transit) brought those same immigrants to homes on the outer fringes of New York City. That tradition has continued as immigrants from around the world have settled close by the no. 7's elevated tracks. Get off in Sunnyside and see Romanian grocery stores and restaurants; a few stops farther in Jackson Heights, you'll see Indians in saris and Sikhs in turbans; go all the way to Flushing and you'll think you are in Chinatown. (You are—Queen's Chinatown is bigger than Manhattan's.) In 1999, the Queens Council on the Arts nominated the International Express for designation as a National Millennium Trail, and that resulted in its selection as representative of the American immigrant experience by the White House Millennium Council, the United States Department of Transportation, and the Rails-to-Trails Conservancy.

fact_check.notes: Sidebar ('The International Express' boxed digression) anchored to MoMI as the nearest narrative POI; subject is the no. 7 line, a non-fixed-point transit route. Superlative 'Queens's Chinatown is bigger than Manhattan's' left to fact-check.

beats.script_body: At this proving ground for young artists, the work is challenging, right of the moment, and sometimes downright wacky. That 'crazy building' in Long Island City was once a public school — hence the name — and its somewhat decrepit charm is part of the experience. Because it's not a fancy white box like its sister institution the Museum of Modern Art, P.S. 1 lets artists create full-blown, sometimes invasive installations; one summer an artist blasted holes in the brick wall of a gallery.

beats.script_body: Long before Google Earth, there was the Panorama of the City of New York — a diorama of 9,335 square feet created for the 1964–65 World's Fair, with the help of photographers who swooped in helicopters over the city, taking over 7,000 photos to capture every building in the five boroughs. Fully updated in 1992, it lets building owners pay to have newer edifices added, which makes for some odd anomalies. It remains the heart of the Queens Museum.

beats.source_passage: Long before there was Google Earth, there was the Panorama of the City of New York. A diorama of 9,335 square feet, it was created for the 1964–65 World's Fair with the help of photographers who swooped in helicopters over the city, taking over 7,000 photos to capture every building in the five boroughs. The Panorama is still a wonder today, and the heart of the Queens Museum. It was fully updated in 1992, and subsequently, building owners can pay to have their newer edifices added, which makes for some odd anomalies.
